title: What Evolution Is
description: The core idea: populations change over time through heritable variation and selection

concepts.title: Darwin's Insight
concepts.contentHtml:
Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, proposing that all life shares common ancestry and that species change over time via natural selection.

Darwin's argument has four logical steps: (1) organisms vary in their traits; (2) variation is heritable; (3) more organisms are born than can survive; (4) those with favourable traits leave more offspring. Over time, favourable traits become more common — populations evolve.

Alfred Russel Wallace independently arrived at the same idea, prompting Darwin to finally publish. Both presented their work simultaneously to the Linnean Society in 1858.

concepts.title: Heritable Variation and Fitness
concepts.contentHtml:
Variation is the raw material of evolution. Individuals in a population differ in morphology, physiology, and behaviour. If this variation has a heritable basis (a genetic cause), it can be passed on.

Fitness in biology means reproductive success — the number of viable, fertile offspring left in the next generation. It's relative to the environment: the same trait can be beneficial in one habitat and harmful in another.

The classic demonstration: in 1850s Britain, the peppered moth (Biston betularia) existed in pale and dark forms. Industrial soot darkened tree bark, making pale moths visible to predators. Within decades, the dark form dominated — directly observed evolution.

concepts.title: Evidence for Evolution
concepts.contentHtml:
Evolution is supported by multiple independent lines of evidence.

  • Fossil record: transitional forms like Tiktaalik (fish-tetrapod link) show gradual change.
  • Comparative anatomy: the human arm, bat wing, whale flipper, and mole forelimb share the same bones (homologous structures), indicating a common ancestor.
  • Molecular evidence: DNA sequences across species confirm evolutionary relationships — humans and chimpanzees share ~98.7% of their DNA.
  • Biogeography: species distribution maps onto geological history.
  • Direct observation: antibiotic resistance in bacteria, beak size changes in Galapagos finches studied by the Grants over 40 years.

title: Mechanisms of Evolution
description: Natural selection, genetic drift, gene flow, and mutation

concepts.title: Types of Natural Selection
concepts.contentHtml:
Natural selection can act on variation in three modes.

Directional selection favours one extreme phenotype — larger body size in a cold climate, for instance. The population mean shifts over generations.

Stabilising selection favours intermediate phenotypes and removes extremes. Human birth weight is a classic example: very small and very large babies have lower survival; intermediate weights are selected for.

Disruptive selection favours both extremes over the intermediate. In African black-bellied seedcracker finches, both large-billed and small-billed individuals outcompete medium-billed birds because there are two distinct seed sizes.

concepts.title: Genetic Drift
concepts.contentHtml:
Genetic drift is random change in allele frequencies due to chance — not selection. It is most powerful in small populations.

The bottleneck effect occurs when a population is drastically reduced (plague, natural disaster), and the survivors' allele frequencies may not represent the original population. Cheetahs experienced a severe bottleneck ~10,000 years ago and are now so genetically uniform that skin grafts between unrelated cheetahs are not rejected.

The founder effect is similar: a small group colonises a new area. Ellis-van Creveld syndrome, a form of dwarfism, is unusually common in the Amish because their founding population was small.

concepts.title: Gene Flow and Sexual Selection
concepts.contentHtml:
Gene flow is the movement of alleles between populations via migration. It reduces genetic differences between populations and can introduce new alleles. The high genetic diversity of humans outside Africa partly reflects repeated pulses of migration and gene flow.

Sexual selection is a special form of natural selection driven by mate choice. Traits can evolve because they attract mates even if they reduce survival — the peacock's tail impedes escape from predators but females prefer large, colourful tails. Ronald Fisher's 'runaway selection' model explains how such traits can escalate rapidly.

Together, natural selection, genetic drift, gene flow, and mutation are the four core mechanisms of evolution.

title: Speciation
description: How one species becomes two — and the boundaries of species concepts

concepts.title: What Is a Species?
concepts.contentHtml:
The most widely used definition is the biological species concept (Ernst Mayr, 1942): a species is a group of organisms that actually or potentially interbreed and are reproductively isolated from other groups.

This fails for asexual organisms, fossils, and cases where species hybridise (like polar bears and grizzlies). Alternative concepts include the morphological species concept (looks different = different species) and the phylogenetic species concept (smallest monophyletic group with a common ancestor).

In practice, species concepts often conflict — the number of recognised species depends partly on which concept is used.

concepts.title: Allopatric and Sympatric Speciation
concepts.contentHtml:
Allopatric speciation occurs when populations are geographically separated. The Grand Canyon split a squirrel population: the Kaibab squirrel on the north rim and Abert's squirrel on the south rim have diverged significantly in ~10,000 years. Darwin's Galapagos finches radiated as finches colonised different islands, evolving into 14+ distinct species from a single founding population.

Sympatric speciation occurs without geographic separation. Apple maggot flies (Rhagoletis pomonella) began colonising introduced apple trees in the 1800s and are diverging from hawthorn-feeding relatives despite occupying the same geographic area, driven by different host preferences.

concepts.title: Reproductive Isolation Mechanisms
concepts.contentHtml:
Speciation requires the evolution of reproductive barriers that prevent interbreeding.

Prezygotic barriers prevent mating or fertilisation: habitat isolation (species use different habitats), temporal isolation (different mating seasons), behavioural isolation (different courtship signals), mechanical isolation (incompatible morphology), and gametic isolation (sperm and eggs incompatible).

Postzygotic barriers reduce hybrid fitness: hybrid inviability (hybrids don't survive), hybrid sterility (mules — horse × donkey — are vigorous but infertile), or hybrid breakdown (hybrid offspring fertile but their offspring are not).

Speciation is typically a gradual process: partial barriers accumulate until two populations can no longer exchange genes.

title: The Tree of Life
description: Phylogenetics, common ancestry, and the history of life on Earth

concepts.title: Reading Phylogenetic Trees
concepts.contentHtml:
A phylogenetic tree (or cladogram) represents the evolutionary history of groups of organisms. Branch points (nodes) represent common ancestors; tips represent living or extinct taxa.

Organisms that share a more recent common ancestor are more closely related. Humans are more closely related to chimpanzees than to gorillas — our lineage diverged from chimps' ~6 million years ago, while the human-chimp lineage split from gorillas ~9 million years ago.

Trees are built from shared derived characters (synapomorphies) — traits that arose in a common ancestor and were inherited by all its descendants.

concepts.title: Major Events in the History of Life
concepts.contentHtml:
Life on Earth spans ~3.8 billion years. Key milestones:

  • ~3.8 Ga: First single-celled life (prokaryotes)
  • ~2.4 Ga: Great Oxygenation Event — cyanobacteria flood atmosphere with O2
  • ~1.8 Ga: First eukaryotes (cells with nuclei)
  • ~600 Ma: First multicellular animals; Ediacaran fauna
  • ~540 Ma: Cambrian Explosion — most animal phyla appear in ~20 million years
  • ~66 Ma: End-Cretaceous mass extinction kills non-avian dinosaurs; mammals diversify

Five mass extinctions have each wiped out >75% of species; life has recovered each time, but often with a very different cast of dominant organisms.

concepts.title: Molecular Clocks and Deep Time
concepts.contentHtml:
DNA accumulates mutations at roughly constant rates. This molecular clock lets scientists estimate when two lineages diverged, even without fossils.

Mitochondrial DNA mutates faster than nuclear DNA and has been used to trace human ancestry. Landmark studies by Cann, Stoneking, and Wilson in 1987 used mtDNA to argue all living humans share a common female ancestor in Africa ~200,000 years ago — 'Mitochondrial Eve'.

Combining molecular clocks with fossil calibration gives the time-calibrated phylogeny — the full evolutionary tree of life with dates. These analyses confirm that all life shares common ancestry and reveal the extraordinary depth of evolutionary time.

title: Evolution in the Modern World
description: Rapid evolution, human evolution, and evo-devo

concepts.title: Antibiotic and Pesticide Resistance
concepts.contentHtml:
Evolution is not just historical — it happens in real time whenever selection pressure is strong. Antibiotic resistance is one of the most urgent public health crises of our era.

When bacteria are exposed to an antibiotic, most die but resistant mutants survive and reproduce. Alexander Fleming, who discovered penicillin, warned in his 1945 Nobel lecture that misuse would breed resistant bacteria. He was right: MRSA (Staphylococcus aureus resistant to methicillin) now kills hundreds of thousands yearly.

Similarly, pesticide-resistant insects and herbicide-resistant weeds evolve wherever chemicals are heavily used — a direct demonstration that natural selection is ongoing and powerful.

concepts.title: Human Evolution
concepts.contentHtml:
The human lineage (Hominini) split from our last common ancestor with chimpanzees ~6–7 million years ago in Africa. Early hominins walked upright but had small brains. Australopithecus afarensis ('Lucy', ~3.2 Ma) was bipedal but ape-brained.

The genus Homo appeared ~2.8 Ma. Homo erectus was the first hominin to leave Africa and had a substantially larger brain. Homo sapiens emerged ~300,000 years ago in Africa; modern human behaviour appeared ~70,000–100,000 years ago.

Ancient DNA has revealed that modern humans interbred with Neanderthals and Denisovans. Non-African humans carry ~1–4% Neanderthal DNA; Melanesians carry up to 6% Denisovan DNA.

concepts.title: Evo-Devo
concepts.contentHtml:
Evolutionary developmental biology (evo-devo) explores how changes in developmental genes drive major evolutionary innovations.

Hox genes are a conserved family of transcription factors that determine body segment identity in animals — a fly Hox gene transplanted into a mouse still functions. Mutations in Hox genes can produce dramatic changes: Antennapedia mutant flies grow legs where antennae should be.

The same toolkit of ~100 developmental genes is found across wildly different animals. Major morphological novelties — wings, eyes, limbs — arose not by inventing new genes but by deploying old ones in new ways. This explains why the Cambrian Explosion was possible: the genetic infrastructure was already in place.

concepts.title: Tree of Life Reconstruction
concepts.contentHtml:
Phylogenetic trees represent evolutionary relationships. Branches show common ancestry; tip species share more recent ancestors with closer neighbors.

Modern phylogenetics is sequence-based: align homologous DNA or protein sequences across species, infer the tree that best explains the data. Likelihood and Bayesian methods quantify uncertainty.

Surprises abound: hippos are closer to whales than to pigs; mushrooms are closer to animals than to plants; placental mammals diversified after the dinosaur extinction.

concepts.title: The Molecular Clock
concepts.contentHtml:
Mutations accumulate at roughly constant rates over time, especially at neutral sites. The number of differences between two sequences scales with their time since divergence.

Calibrate the clock from fossil dates; then estimate divergence times for any branch. Modern Homo sapiens diverged from chimps ~6 Mya; primates and rodents ~80 Mya; eukaryotes ~2 Gya.

Different genes tick at different rates, and rates can vary across lineages. Bayesian methods now estimate divergence times more carefully, with uncertainty bounds.

concepts.title: Horizontal Gene Transfer
concepts.contentHtml:
The 'tree' of life isn't always a clean tree. Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) — genes jumping between species — is rampant in bacteria and archaea, and occurs occasionally in eukaryotes.

Antibiotic resistance plasmids spread by HGT in days. Mitochondria and chloroplasts came from bacterial endosymbionts billions of years ago — wholesale gene transfer. Even some animal genes (like aphid carotenoid biosynthesis) appear to have come from fungi by HGT.

The early tree of life is more like a network. Reconstructing prokaryotic evolution requires explicit HGT models.

concepts.title: What Counts as a Major Transition?
concepts.contentHtml:
Maynard Smith and Szathmáry (1995) catalogued the major transitions in evolution — events where new levels of biological organization arose. Examples:

• Replicating molecules → cells.
• Independent replicators → chromosomes.
• Prokaryotes → eukaryotes (endosymbiosis).
• Asexual → sexual reproduction.
• Single cells → multicellularity.
• Solitary individuals → eusocial colonies.
• Primate societies → human language and culture.

Each transition involved cooperation, division of labor, and integration of formerly independent units.

concepts.title: The Eukaryotic Cell
concepts.contentHtml:
Eukaryotic cells arose from a fusion of an archaeal host cell and a bacterial endosymbiont (~1.5-2 Gya). The bacterium became the mitochondrion. A second endosymbiosis with cyanobacteria gave plants their chloroplasts.

Lynn Margulis pushed endosymbiotic theory in the 1960s, against initial resistance. Today it's textbook biology, supported by overwhelming molecular evidence.

Why eukaryotic cells didn't evolve again is debated — the mitochondrion provided enough energy to maintain a complex genome, and that may have been a hard-to-cross threshold.

concepts.title: Multicellularity & Eusociality
concepts.contentHtml:
Multicellularity has evolved many times — animals, plants, fungi, and several lineages of algae. Each is an integration of formerly independent cells via signaling, adhesion, and differentiation.

Eusociality — colonies with reproductive division of labor — has evolved in ants, bees, wasps, termites, naked mole-rats, some shrimp. Workers forgo direct reproduction; the colony reproduces as a unit.

Both transitions involve resolving evolutionary conflicts (cheaters can be selected for) — through kin selection, policing, and barriers to defection.

concepts.title: Evo-Devo Discoveries
concepts.contentHtml:
Evolutionary developmental biology (evo-devo) showed that the same genes control development across vast evolutionary distances. Hox genes pattern body segments in flies, fish, mice, and us — in roughly the same order on the chromosome.

Pax6 induces eye development in flies and mice. Sonic hedgehog patterns limbs across all vertebrates. The same toolkit, redeployed.

Implication: dramatic morphological evolution often comes not from new genes but from changes in when and where existing genes are expressed — regulatory evolution.

concepts.title: Phenotypic Plasticity & Evolvability
concepts.contentHtml:
An organism's response to environment (plasticity) can shape its evolution. Genetic accommodation: traits initially produced by environment can become genetically fixed if persistently advantageous.

Evolvability — the capacity to generate adaptive variation — itself evolves. Modular development, redundant gene networks, and regulatory hubs increase evolvability.

The 'Extended Evolutionary Synthesis' debates how much these phenomena revise the modern synthesis. Most biologists agree they enrich it; how fundamentally is contested.

concepts.title: Frontiers
concepts.contentHtml:
Ancient DNA: techniques pioneered by Pääbo (Nobel 2022) recovered Neanderthal genomes and showed Homo sapiens interbred with Neanderthals and Denisovans — modern non-Africans carry 1-4% Neanderthal DNA.

Experimental evolution: Lenski's E. coli have evolved in flasks for >75,000 generations, accumulating beneficial mutations. Direct observation of evolution in action.

Synthetic biology creates organisms with redesigned genomes — minimal cells (JCVI-syn3.0), expanded genetic codes, engineered metabolisms. The line between studying and creating life is blurring.
